extracted.intended_audience: recipients of federal financial assistance (schools, colleges, universities), Title IX coordinators, higher-education administrators, and Title IX compliance staff
extracted.subtask_description: Preamble guidance and regulatory clarifications defining actionable sexual harassment under Title IX, including how to evaluate 'objectively offensive', the 'effectively denies equal access' element, and which offenses are per se sexual harassment. Intended to direct schools' investigatory, training, and remedial obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectively offensive evaluated under a reasonable person standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether harassing conduct is 'objectively offensive' must be evaluated under a reasonable person standard, as a reasonable person in the complainant's position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The objective inquiry means a reasonable person standing in the complainant's shoes would find the conduct offensive; this does not make the phrase oxymoronic. The standard should not result in blaming victims or excluding support when evaluators differ in race, sex, age, or other characteristics from the complainant. It is inappropriate for Title IX personnel to dismiss conduct as 'boys being boys' or otherwise apply bias when evaluating objective offensiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Both subjective and objective elements retained (Davis formulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Actionable harassment turns on both subjectivity (whether the conduct is unwelcome to the complainant) and objectivity ('objectively offensive'), with the Davis elements determined under a reasonable person standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This preserves the 'both subjective and objective' analytic approach used in prior guidance while adapting the Supreme Court's Davis framework for administrative enforcement. The Department declined to add an intent element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not require consideration of male/female perspectives separately
rubrics_metrics.description: The reasonable person standard is evaluated as a reasonable person in the complainant's position; the Department will not require evaluators to separately consider offensiveness from both male and female perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requiring separate male/female perspective consideration would invite application of sex stereotypes; evaluation must avoid sex-based stereotyping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid bias and unconscious bias in evaluations and trainings
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients have flexibility in designing Title IX personnel training, and such training may address implicit or unconscious bias so that bias does not improperly influence evaluation of what conduct is 'offensive.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nothing in the final regulations precludes training on implicit bias. Title IX Coordinators and investigatory personnel must avoid prejudiced assumptions that could evidence sex-based bias in contravention of §106.45(a) or bias for/against a party under §106.45(b)(1)(iii).

rubrics_metrics.name: No intent element required for actionable harassment
rubrics_metrics.description: The Davis standard does not require proof of the respondent's intent; unwelcome conduct that is severe, pervasive, and objectively offensive enough to deny equal educational opportunity is actionable regardless of intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not requiring intent prevents perpetrators from excusing conduct by claiming lack of intent; evaluators focus on impact, not subjective intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregate/cumulative-impact analysis (reject disaggregation of allegations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective offensiveness is analyzed from the perspective of a reasonable person in the complainant's shoes, using an approach that rejects disaggregation and instead looks at the aggregate or cumulative impact of conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisionmakers should consider the totality of circumstances—small, repeated microaggressions or 'inside' jokes that together harm a complainant may meet the standard even if individual incidents seem minor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectively denies a person equal access — definition and measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: The second prong requires that the conduct 'effectively denies a person equal access' to the recipient's education program or activity, measured against the access of a person not subjected to the harassment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This element does not require total exclusion or that the complainant has already withdrawn or failed classes. Signs may include skipping class to avoid a harasser, decline in GPA, or difficulty concentrating; no particular manifestation of trauma is required. The focus is on denial of 'equal' access, not a requirement of 'constructive expulsion.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify 'equal' modifier throughout regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: References to denial/preservation/restoration of access must include the modifier 'equal' (e.g., 'effectively denies equal access', 'restore or preserve equal access') to align with §106.30's definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent use of 'equal' ensures appropriate interpretation: Title IX protects equal access to education, not total denial in every case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hostile environment concept replaced/adapted by 'denial of equal access' for Title IX
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations frame actionable harassment in terms of denying equal access to education rather than adopting the broader workplace-origin 'hostile environment' concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While hostile environment and denial of equal access may overlap, the denial-of-equal-access formulation is tailored to Title IX's non-discrimination focus and better accommodates free-speech and academic-freedom concerns. Title IX is not a federal civility code and need not prohibit every instance of unwelcome conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Per se sexual harassment: include Clery Act/VAWA offenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Every incident of the Clery Act/VAWA offenses — sexual assault, dating violence, domestic violence, and stalking — is included as per se sexual harassment under prong (3) of §106.30.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because these offenses concern non-expressive, often violent conduct, they are inherently serious sex-based offenses that risk equal educational access and therefore should not be subjected to the Davis severity/pervasiveness scrutiny; a single instance can be actionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single instances of dating violence, domestic violence, and stalking can be actionable
rubrics_metrics.description: Dating violence, domestic violence, and stalking are recognized as sufficiently serious that even a single incident should not have to meet the Davis standard to be covered by Title IX.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department agreed with commenters that failing to remediate single incidents of these offenses risks escalation and significant harm; recipients should treat these offenses as automatically within §106.30's scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients must offer supportive measures and implement remedies to restore/preserve equal access
rubrics_metrics.description: When sexual harassment effectively denies a person equal access, recipients must offer supportive measures designed to restore or preserve the complainant's equal educational access, and when a grievance process finds a respondent responsible, recipients must implement remedies to restore or preserve equal access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supportive measures and remedies should focus on restoring equal access; this is a procedural obligation embedded in §106.30 and related provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different fact-specific conclusions across schools are permissible
rubrics_metrics.description: Because evaluating sexual harassment is fact-specific, different people or institutions may reach different conclusions about similar conduct; that variability is not inherently unreasonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department does not consider some divergence in outcomes problematic given differing facts and circumstances, and maintains flexibility for recipients in certain policy/training choices (subject to anti-bias and non-discrimination constraints).
